```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_xgboost = requireNamespace("xgboost", quietly = TRUE)
has_sklearn = requireNamespace("reticulate", quietly = TRUE) && reticulate::py_module_available("sklearn")
```

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(rml)
set.seed(7)
n = 2000
X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = runif(n),
               region = sample(c('north', 'south', 'east', 'west'), n, replace = TRUE),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
region_effect = c(north = 1, south = -1, east = 0.5, west = 0)[X$region]
y = as.numeric(runif(n) < 1/(1 + exp(-(X$x1 - X$x2^2 + region_effect))))
train = sample(n, 1500)
```

## How transformers work

Every model has a list of `transformers`. A transformer is itself a model. When the parent model is
fitted, it

1. fits each of its transformers on the same `X` and `y`,
2. calls their `predict()` and binds the outputs column-wise,
3. trains itself on those columns.

At prediction the same chain runs again, so a single `predict()` call evaluates the whole network. A
transformer can have its own transformers, so models can be nested to any depth.

With no transformers a model is trained on the raw columns. With transformers it only sees what they
output. To keep the raw columns as well, add the identity mapper `MAP.RML.IDT`:

```{r idt}
model = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'lr', verbose = 0,
  transformers = list(MAP.RML.IDT(name = 'I', features.include = c('x1', 'x2', 'x3')),
                      ENC.RML.TE(name = 'te')))   # target encoder for the categorical column
model$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
model$objects$features$fname
model$performance(X[-train, ], y[-train], metrics = 'gini')
```

The column names show where each feature came from: `I_x1` is column `x1` passed by transformer `I`,
and `te_region` is the target-encoded region. Set `verbose = 0` on each model to silence its progress
messages (the setting is not inherited by transformers).

## Models as features (stacking)

Any classifier or regressor can be a transformer. Its prediction becomes a feature of the parent.
Use `return = 'logit'` for classifier transformers that feed linear models.

```{r stacking, eval = has_xgboost}
stack = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'stack', verbose = 0,
  transformers = list(
    CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgb', nrounds = 50, max_depth = 3, return = 'logit', verbose = 0,
                transformers = list(MAP.RML.IDT(name = 'I', features.include = c('x1', 'x2', 'x3')), ENC.RML.TE(name = 'te'))),
    MAP.RML.IDT(name = 'raw', features.include = c('x1', 'x2'))))
stack$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
stack$objects$features
stack$performance(X[-train, ], y[-train], metrics = 'gini')
```

`info.transformers()` lists the nodes of the network:

```{r info, eval = has_xgboost}
stack$info.transformers()[, c('name', 'type', 'class', 'outputs', 'fitted')]
```

## What a transformer passes on

By default a model's `predict()` returns only its own output columns. Two switches change that:

| Setting | Effect on the output |
| --- | --- |
| `keep_columns = TRUE` | Also returns the input columns the model did **not** use. |
| `keep_features = TRUE` | Also returns the input columns the model **did** use. |
| `pass_columns` | With either switch on, only these input columns are passed. |
| `remove_columns` | With either switch on, these input columns are never passed. |

```{r keep}
scaler = MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z', keep_columns = TRUE)
scaler$fit(X)
head(scaler$predict(X), 3)
```

## Choosing columns before and after transformation

* `features.include` / `features.exclude` filter the **input** columns before they reach the transformers.
* `features.include.at` / `features.exclude.at` filter the columns **after** transformation, just before
  the model trains.
* `column_filters` removes features by their statistics. The default removes constant columns:
  `list(list(column = 'n_unique', filter = ' > 1'))`. With `eda.enabled = TRUE` more statistics
  (moments, quantiles, missing counts) are available to filter on.

```{r at}
m = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'lr_at', verbose = 0,
  transformers = list(MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z'), MAP.RML.MMS(name = 'm')),
  features.include = c('x1', 'x2', 'x3'),
  features.exclude.at = c('m_x3'))
m$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
m$objects$features$fname
```

## Building blocks

| Type | Classes | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mappers | `MAP.RML.IDT`, `MAP.RML.ZFS`, `MAP.RML.MMS`, `MAP.STATS.PCA`, `MAP.SKLEARN.*` | Pass, scale or project numeric columns |
| Encoders | `ENC.RML.TE`, `ENC.RML.FE`, `ENC.RML.ME`, `ENC.SKLEARN.OHE`, `ENC.FASTDUMMIES.OHE`, `ENC.CATEGORY_ENCODERS.*` | Turn categorical columns into numbers |
| Binners | `BIN.RML.OBB`, `BIN.KMEANS.KMC`, `BIN.SKLEARN.KMC`, `BIN.SMBINNING.OB` | Cut numeric columns into bins or clusters |
| Feature generators | `FET.RML.D2MUL`, `FET.SKLEARN.MFG` | Pairwise products, polynomial features |
| Function transformers | `FNT.RML.LOG`, `FNT.RML.INV`, `FNT.RML.LOGIT` | Apply a fixed function to each column |
| Ensemblers | `ENS.RML.AGGR`, `ENS.RML.BS` | Aggregate model outputs, or pick one model per row |
| Clustering and grouping | `BIN.KMEANS.KMC`, `BIN.SKLEARN.KMC`, `BIN.RML.GROUPER`, `CATCONCATER` | Cluster rows, group or combine categories |

`vignette('rml-transformers')` shows each of these on its own and `vignette('rml-ensembles-and-tools')`
covers the ensemblers.

An ensemble of three models averaged by `ENS.RML.AGGR`:

```{r ensemble, eval = has_xgboost}
ens = ENS.RML.AGGR(name = 'avg', aggregator = 'mean', verbose = 0,
  transformers = list(
    CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'a', features.include = c('x1', 'x2')),
    CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'b', verbose = 0, transformers = list(ENC.RML.TE(name = 'te'), MAP.RML.IDT(name = 'I', features.include = 'x1'))),
    CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'c', nrounds = 30, features.include = c('x1', 'x2', 'x3'))))
ens$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
ens$performance(X[-train, ], y[-train], metrics = 'gini')
```

## Python models

Classes with `SKLEARN` in their name wrap scikit-learn through reticulate. Arguments are passed to the
scikit-learn constructor; whole numbers are sent to Python as integers, so `n_neighbors = 25` works. If R cannot find the Python module,
see `vignette('rml-troubleshooting')`.

```{r sklearn, eval = has_sklearn}
knn = CLS.SKLEARN.KNN(name = 'knn', n_neighbors = 25, verbose = 0,
                      transformers = list(MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z', features.include = c('x1', 'x2', 'x3'))))
knn$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
knn$performance(X[-train, ], y[-train], metrics = 'gini')
```

## Training transformers in parallel

Set `mc.num_cores` on the parent to fit and run its transformers on several cores (requires the
doParallel package). Each worker loads rml, so it must be installed, not just sourced.

```{r parallel, eval = FALSE}
model = CLS.STATS.LR(mc.num_cores = 4, transformers = list(...))
```

## Failed transformers

If a transformer fails to fit, the parent prints a warning and removes it (`remove_failed_transformers =
TRUE`, the default), then trains on the remaining outputs. The error is kept in
`transformer$objects$fitting_error`.

## Random model search with templates

`build_model_from_template()` creates a random model from a named list of templates. A template gives
the class, value ranges for its arguments, and which transformers it may get and how likely each is.
The package ships `default_templates`.

```{r templates, eval = has_xgboost}
set.seed(1)
candidate = build_model_from_template('CLS.XGBOOST', templates = default_templates)
candidate$config[c('nrounds', 'max_depth', 'eta')]
length(candidate$transformers)
```
